baseline_incident_edges.relationship: History beyond dynastic courts, joined to civic and national renewal (1901–1903)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Dirlik’s epilogue discusses Liang’s 1902 programme; the authorized Renewing the People excerpt describes renewal as a selective combination of inherited and acquired resources. Zheng traces the changing national vocabulary. This does not equate civic renewal with one fixed ethnic nationalism.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Qing scholarship reinterpreted as a Chinese renaissance (1920), in Blitstein’s reading
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Blitstein, pp. 180–182, contrasts Liang’s recovery of the Qing intellectual past with Hu Shi’s future-oriented renaissance. The statement is mediated by this named reader; no universal equation between Chinese and European histories follows.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Dirlik credits the break with inherited historiography but questions its comprehensive explanatory framework (1978)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Dirlik’s introduction, pp. 3–4, argues that Liang’s and Gu’s innovations did not supply a replacement general theory; the epilogue distinguishes social history and document criticism. This is Dirlik’s appraisal routed through Marxist historiography, not a collective rejection of Liang.
